oneSentence: A label for AI models near the current leading edge of capability or scale, especially those seen as pushing technical limits and raising new governance questions.
plainExplanation:
People use this label for AI models that sit near the leading edge of what current systems can do. They are usually very large machine learning systems trained on vast datasets, and they can often handle many different tasks such as writing, coding, summarising, analysing images, or translating text. The boundary is not fixed. What counts as “frontier” changes as technology moves on.

What goes in is usually a prompt, image, audio clip, or other input. Inside the system, the model uses patterns learned from training data to produce an output, such as the next word, a label, a translation, or generated content. What comes out can look impressive, but it is still generated from statistical pattern matching rather than guaranteed fact.

The term is often confused with foundation model. A foundation model is a broad base model that can be adapted to many uses. A frontier model is a relative label: it points to the most advanced models available at a certain moment. Many frontier models are also foundation models, but not every foundation model is frontier.

The term is also often confused with artificial general intelligence, or AGI. Frontier models may perform strongly across many tasks, but that does not mean they have human-like general intelligence, consciousness, or reliable judgement. The word “frontier” says more about current capability and potential impact than about the system having a mind or broad understanding like a person.

everydayAnalogy.title: This year's flagship phone
everydayAnalogy.story: A new flagship phone may have the strongest camera, fastest processor and widest range of features currently available. That places it near the leading edge today, but next year's devices may move the edge. Being the flagship also does not mean every photograph will be accurate, every feature will work equally well or the phone is suitable for every user. Frontier model is similarly a comparative and time-dependent label, not a quality guarantee.

mapping.analogyElement: The newest and strongest booth in the building
mapping.aiElement: A model considered among the most capable available at that time
Prompts or other inputs such as text, audio, or images

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A translation booth is a single visible machine built for one clear purpose. Frontier models are not one kind of device, and they may generate text, images, code, or predictions across many tasks. Also, the analogy may suggest that “frontier” is an official technical threshold, when in practice the boundary is debated and shifts over time.

visual.title: Foundation model, frontier model, and AGI are not the same label
visual.learningObjective: After viewing, the reader should be able to explain that “frontier” is a moving label for leading capability, not a fixed technical category and not the same as AGI.
visual.description: A three-column comparison. Read left to right: a broad reusable model, a current leading-edge model, and a hypothetical human-level general system. Arrows show overlap between the first two, and a clear gap between frontier models and AGI claims.

steps.label: Foundation model
steps.explanation: A broad model that can be adapted to many tasks. It is defined by reuse across applications, not by being the strongest available.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a left column box labelled 'Foundation model'. Inside, place small icons for text, image, code, and speech. Add a note: 'general-purpose base model'.

steps.label: Frontier model
steps.explanation: A model described as near the current limit of capability or scale. This is a relative status that can change as newer systems appear.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a centre column box labelled 'Frontier model'. Use a highlighted outline. Add a timeline marker above it reading 'current leading edge'. Include the same task icons plus a note: 'moves over time'.

steps.label: Overlap
steps.explanation: Many frontier models are also foundation models, because the most advanced systems are often broad and reusable. But not every foundation model is frontier.
steps.visualInstruction: Add a double-headed arrow between the first and second columns. Beneath it, write 'often overlaps, not identical'.

steps.label: Not the same as AGI
steps.explanation: Strong performance across many tasks does not prove human-like general intelligence, consciousness, or dependable judgement in all settings.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a right column box labelled 'AGI'. Use a dashed border and a note: 'hypothetical or contested concept'. Add a clear separator line between the frontier and AGI columns labelled 'not equivalent'.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping each column reveals a short tooltip with the column definition and one 'not the same as' clarification.
visual.accessibilityDescription: This comparison diagram has three columns. The first column is 'Foundation model' and shows a broad base model reused for text, images, code, and speech. The second column is 'Frontier model' and shows a highlighted current leading-edge model with the note that the label moves over time. An arrow between the first and second columns says they often overlap but are not identical. The third column is 'AGI' with a dashed border and the note that it is a hypothetical or contested concept. A separator between the second and third columns states that frontier models are not equivalent to AGI.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static three-column comparison with visible notes and labels instead of hover effects. All definitions and distinctions are shown at once.

workedExample.scenario: An information management officer at a regional hub must circulate an options note before an ICT governance board meets on Monday. To distinguish capability from marketing, the officer compares candidate models using a synthetic pack containing long texts, charts, photographs and short audio clips.
workedExample.input: A synthetic and public test pack, with tasks covering multilingual summarisation, chart interpretation, image description and comparison of information across formats.
process: The officer applies the same test pack and scoring criteria to each candidate model.
One model performs near the current leading edge across several tasks and data types, while the others are narrower or less consistent.
The leading model still invents a chart label, misses context in an audio clip and produces uneven results in one language.
The options note describes it provisionally as a frontier model and records when the assessment was made, since the label will shift as capabilities advance.
The board considers the model's errors, deployment arrangements and controls separately from its frontier status.
workedExample.result: The options note uses frontier as a time-bound description of comparative capability. It does not treat the label as evidence that the model is accurate, safe, approved or suitable for every task.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: Before rotating out, a communications officer in a Headquarters department must complete a handover note by close of business on Friday. It covers a pilot tool whose vendor describes its text-and-image model as frontier, including tests on cleared public statements and photographs and the questions still awaiting the ICT governance board.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Frontier describes a model's position near the current leading edge, not its suitability for the department's work. The label is relative, may soon become dated and should be tested against the capabilities actually needed. The adjective does not clear the tool for use.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload embargoed statements, personal data, unpublished photographs or security-sensitive material to a model not approved for that material. A frontier label says nothing about retention, secondary use, access controls or confidentiality.

whyItMatters: For policy and leadership, this term often appears in risk, procurement, competition, and governance discussions. It can influence how people judge opportunity and danger. If you treat it as a precise scientific category, you may overestimate what a system can reliably do. If you ignore it, you may miss why some models attract special attention: they can be more capable, more widely deployable, and potentially more consequential than earlier systems. The key decision point is not whether a model is called frontier, but what evidence exists about its performance, limits, safety controls, access model, and appropriate uses.
whereYouMayHearIt: A vendor demo during a procurement unit's market consultation
An ICT governance board reviewing an options note
An inter-agency working group discussing AI governance
A Headquarters briefing before senior leadership considers a pilot

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A frontier model is simply any model with a very large number of parameters.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Size often matters, but the label is not based on one number. People use it for systems seen as near the leading edge of capability, scale, or impact at a given time. A smaller model could outperform a larger one on some tasks, and a large model may not be leading once better systems appear.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model is called frontier, its answers are probably correct.
commonMisconceptions.correction: The label points to capability, not guaranteed accuracy. A frontier model may produce fluent summaries, code, or translations while still making factual errors, missing context, or giving unsuitable outputs. Stronger performance reduces some failures but does not remove the need for testing and human oversight.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Frontier model means the same thing as AGI.
commonMisconceptions.correction: No settled definition makes those terms identical. Frontier models are current leading systems; AGI usually refers to a hypothetical system with much broader, more human-like general capability. People disagree on AGI definitions, so using 'frontier' does not prove that such a threshold has been reached.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A frontier model is one of the most advanced AI models available right now. It can often do many tasks well, but it is still a tool with limits and should not be treated as automatically reliable or human-like.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In technical and policy use, 'frontier model' is a relative and time-dependent label for models near the current state of the art in capability, scale, or generality, often with potential for broad deployment and significant downstream effects. In practice, these are commonly large deep learning models trained on extensive datasets with substantial compute, and many are multimodal, meaning they can process more than one data type such as text and images. Inputs may include prompts, images, audio, or structured data; the model transforms these inputs into probability-based outputs such as generated text, classifications, translations, or action recommendations. The term does not identify one universal architecture, benchmark, parameter count, or legal category. It is also not equivalent to 'foundation model', although there is frequent overlap, and it is not evidence of artificial general intelligence.

keyTakeaway: A frontier model is near today's leading edge of capability, scale or generality. It is a moving label, not a certification of accuracy, safety or fitness for use.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best captures what 'frontier model' usually means?
options: A model near the current leading edge of capability, often broad in use, but still requiring evidence and oversight
Any model that is open-source and available for anyone to download
A model that has reached human-like general intelligence across all domains
Any automated system used in government or large organisations
quickCheck.explanation: The term is usually used for models seen as among the most capable available at a given time. It is relative, not permanent. It does not mean the model is open-source, fully reliable, or equivalent to AGI.

searchKeywords: what is a frontier ai model
contested: The definition is genuinely contested. Different organisations and commentators use 'frontier model' differently: some emphasise capability, some scale or compute, some deployment impact, and some focus on risk. There is no single universally accepted threshold.

issues.problem: The definition makes being general-purpose part of the label. Usage is not that consistent. A model may be described as frontier because it is near a capability or scale boundary without being broadly general-purpose. This also conflicts with the page's later, broader description based on capability, scale, or impact.
issues.fix: A label for AI models near the current leading edge of capability or scale, especially those seen as pushing technical limits and raising new governance questions.

issues.problem: The model does not predict a "useful" output. Usefulness is not what the prediction process guarantees. It produces an output based on learned statistical relationships, and that output may be useful or useless.
issues.fix: Replace "predict a useful output" with "produce an output".

issues.problem: The organisation compares only two models, then classifies one as frontier "for their evaluation." Frontier is not a label for whichever model wins a local two-model comparison. The example asserts that it is near the top of currently available systems without showing evidence for that comparison. There is no arithmetic result to verify: 12 reports, 100 words, three trends, two unsupported claims, and one mistranslation are stated independently and are never combined in a calculation.
issues.fix: They call it the stronger model in this evaluation. That result alone does not establish that it is a frontier model, and they still require human review before use.

issues.problem: The result continues to treat the local test as support for the frontier label. It also says the drafts are faster without reporting any time comparison.
issues.fix: The team gets draft summaries and translations, but not publication-ready material. This test compares local performance and does not by itself establish that a model is frontier, trustworthy, or autonomous.

issues.problem: The absolute claim that the term does not name a legal category is unsafe. A particular legal or policy framework may define such a category even though there is no single universal definition. The page can deny a universal category, not every context-specific legal category.
issues.fix: Replace "The term does not name a single architecture, benchmark threshold, parameter count, or legal category" with "The term does not identify one universal architecture, benchmark, parameter count, or legal category".

issues.problem: Option 0 is the only defensible answer. Option 1 describes availability rather than capability but imprecisely says "open-source" instead of testing the listed distinction from an open-weight model. Option 2 plainly substitutes AGI and adds the extreme claim "across all domains." Option 3 is unrelated to any plausible meaning. The repeated "any" and "all" absolutes make the answer obvious without requiring a sound distinction.
issues.fix: Use these distractors: "A leading model whose trained weights are publicly released"; "A broad model whose strong performance proves reliable human-like judgement"; "A broad model that can be adapted to many different tasks".

issues.problem: The explanation says "open-source," but the relevant distinct term supplied for this page is "open-weight." Those terms are not interchangeable, so the explanation fails to make the required distinction precisely.
issues.fix: The term is usually used for models seen as among the most capable available at a given time. It is relative, not permanent. It does not mean the model's weights are public, that it is fully reliable, or that it is equivalent to AGI.
